**[!!] PREFILL-ON-PREFILL REFUTED, AND THE INTERFERENCE IS CROSS-BLOCK -- which rules out shared
memory entirely (2026-10-10). 26th elimination, and it redirects the whole search.**

| arm | prefill items/CTA | decode items in grid | fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DEC_ROWS=1 SM_SPLIT=all` (control) | ~0.4 | 7 | **0/6** |
| **`DEC_ROWS=1 SM_SPLIT=8`** | **~7** | **7** | **0/6 -- CLEAN** |
| `DEC_ROWS=128 SM_SPLIT=all` (known) | ~7 on 8 blocks | **896** | 6/6 at ~100 bad rows |

**Packing the 56 prefill items onto 8 blocks at ~7 each, with essentially no decode work, is
CLEAN.** The density is the same as the corrupting configuration; the decode item COUNT is not. So:

1. **Prefill-on-prefill cross-item interference is REFUTED** -- my framing from the previous entry,
   dead one arm later.
2. **`>1 work item per CTA` is NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT.** The threshold sweep's "clean 15/15
   below 1 item/CTA" still holds, but density alone does not reproduce the defect. What tracks it is
   the **total number of decode items in the grid**.
3. **[!] THEREFORE THE INTERFERENCE IS CROSS-BLOCK.** The plan decode showed the corrupted blocks
   are ~94% prefill (6-8 FULL vs 0-1 PART items), so the 896 decode items live on OTHER blocks. A
   block's decode items cannot touch another block's shared memory. **That eliminates `smem_q`,
   `sO`/`smem_v`, the K/V stages and every other shared-memory mechanism as the ROUTE** -- they can
   only ever be contributors within a block, which is exactly how the two confirmed ones behaved
   (partial and depth-scoped).

**The suspect list is now global/device state, and the fused kernel has one that stock does not:**
the **`cluster_cursor` backfill queue** -- `fused_plan.cuh`'s *"one device-side cursor every block
pulls persistent cluster indices from once its own work is done: this is what lets an SM that
finished FA3 backfill the tile-16 queue instead of idling"*. With 896 decode items there is heavy
backfill; with 7 there is almost none. That matches the measured dependence exactly, is cross-block
by construction, is a race by construction (an atomic cursor), and is **ours, not stock's** -- which
also explains why stock-configured arms fail at a much lower rate rather than never.

Other global candidates, ranked: `num_pers_clusters` / the persistent cluster list; `merge_indptr` /
`merge_o_indices` sizing (though `FUSED_NOSPLIT=1` did not help, which weakens the slab); and the
`fa3_batch_list` compaction.

**Next test, and it is a single knob:** the backfill is what `cluster_cursor` exists for. Disable
backfill (or set `num_pers_clusters = 0`) at `DEC_ROWS=128 SM_SPLIT=all` -- the configuration that
fails 6/6. If it goes clean, the backfill queue is the route and 26 eliminations resolve to one
mechanism that is entirely our own addition.

**[x] PER-ITEM-TYPE ACCOUNTING BALANCES (25th elimination) -- AND IT KILLS MY AGGRESSOR/VICTIM
STORY: THE CORRUPTED BLOCKS ARE NEARLY PURE PREFILL (2026-10-10).**

Split the register counters into full-tile (`qo_len >= CTA_Q`) and partial-tile populations, so an
imbalance between them cannot cancel in a block sum:

```
verdict: bad rows 120/384          <- still fails; instrument does not mask
ASYM threads: 0
blocks with both lines: 132
blocks where FULL or PART disagrees: 0
blocks with FULL items > 0: 8      (values 6, 7, 8  ->  8 x ~7 = 56 = the prefill item count)
```

1. **The FULL population WAS exercised** -- 8 blocks hold all 56 prefill items -- and
   `FULL loaded == FULL cons` in every one. So the per-item-type desync is **refuted**, not
   vacuously but on the blocks that actually carry prefill work. 25th elimination.
2. **[!] AND THOSE 8 BLOCKS ARE NEARLY PURE PREFILL: 6-8 FULL items against 0-1 PART items.**

**That kills the aggressor/victim framing from the previous entry.** I concluded that *"decode items
are the aggressor, prefill the victim"* because corruption lives in prefill items and grows with
`DEC_ROWS`. But prefill and decode items are **not co-resident**: the corrupted blocks run almost
exclusively prefill. A decode item cannot corrupt a prefill item through shared CTA state if it is
not sharing the CTA. **Retracted.**

**The `DEC_ROWS` threshold has a better explanation, and it needs no interaction at all.** Adding
decode rows does not inject an aggressor -- it **crowds the plan**. With 128 decode rows there are
896 decode items, so the LPT splitter packs the 56 prefill items into **8 blocks at ~7 each** instead
of spreading them one-per-block. That pushes those blocks past **1 item per CTA**, which is the
threshold the sweep measured (clean 15/15 below it). So:

* the defect is **prefill-on-prefill cross-item interference**, among the 6-8 prefill items a
  crowded block runs back to back;
* `DEC_ROWS` is a **knob on prefill density per block**, not a source of interfering work;
* and this is consistent with every surviving constraint -- wrong KV tile of the item's own request
  (all 7 items on such a block belong to request 0), warp-quantised damage, 4x depth scaling, and
  the items/CTA threshold.

**This also explains why the earlier `mix_decode` framing kept misleading me:** the fixture's name
and the `DEC_ROWS` sweep both suggest decode work is participating, and it is not -- it is only
changing how densely request 0's own q tiles are packed onto a CTA.

**[!] EARLY-`continue` DEAD BY ARITHMETIC -- and it exposes a GAP IN MY OWN ACCOUNTING
INSTRUMENT (2026-10-10).**

The leading candidate from the previous entry was the `q_tile_idx * CTA_Q >= qo_len` early-exit.
**A decode item never reaches it:** `q_tile_idx = 0`, `packed_qo = 1 token x G4 = 4`, so
`0 >= 4` is false. Checked before building a test; dead.

What the same arithmetic shows instead is the real asymmetry:

| item | tokens | packed_qo | q tiles | tile occupancy | MMA warps with real rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| prefill | 256 | 1024 | 8 | 128/128 = **100%** | **8 of 8** |
| decode | 1 | 4 | 1 | 4/128 = **3%** | **1 of 8** (partially) |

A decode item runs a **full 15-16 tile kv sequence** to produce **4 packed rows**.

**[!] THE GAP: my per-item accounting could not have seen a desync of this shape.** `PIPE_COUNT`
compared, per BLOCK, the producer's summed `num_kv_tiles` against the consumer's release count from
**one thread**, aggregated over all items that block ran. A decode item over-releasing by *k* and a
prefill item under-releasing by *k* **cancels exactly** in that sum, and the instrument reports 0
mismatches -- which it did, on 132/132 blocks. So "loads == consumes" bounds the block TOTAL and says
nothing about per-item-TYPE balance. That is precisely the asymmetry the prefill/decode localisation
now points at, and my strongest-looking synchronisation result does not exclude it.

**The corrected instrument is a small change to the one that already works:** keep the register
counters, but accumulate them into **two** pairs -- one for items with `packed_qo >= CTA_Q` (full
tiles) and one for items with `packed_qo < CTA_Q` (partial tiles) -- and report both per block. If
the partial-tile pair and the full-tile pair disagree in opposite directions, the desync is found and
named. This is the register-accumulate pattern that demonstrably does not mask the defect (124/384
with it enabled), so it is usable as-is.

**Why this is the leading mechanism now:** the consumer's loop bounds derive from `qo_len`
(`n_masking_steps = CAUSAL ? ceil_div(CTA_Q, CTA_KV) : 0`, and the three loops' `kv_tile_idx`
conditions), while the producer's trip count derives from `get_num_kv_tiles`. For a 3%-occupied tile
those two can legitimately differ in ways they cannot for a full tile -- and a per-item imbalance
that cancels in the block sum is exactly what would desync the pipeline for the NEXT item on that
CTA, making a prefill victim re-read a wrong tile of its own request while never importing decode
data. That is the full measured signature, from one mechanism.

**[x][!!] LOCALISED, REPRODUCIBLY: ALL corruption is in the PREFILL items, ZERO in the 896
DECODE-row items -- and the decode items are the AGGRESSOR, the prefill tiles the VICTIM
(2026-10-10). Host-side decode, ALL bad rows mapped, two repeats.**

| | repeat 1 | repeat 2 |
|---|---|---|
| verdict | 104/384 | 88/384 |
| culprit items | **56** of 952 | **49** of 952 |
| by `q_tile` | 7 each, all 8 tiles | 7 each, 7 tiles |
| by `kv_head` | 8 each, all 7 heads | 7 each, all 7 heads |
| **decode-row culprits (items >= 56)** | **0** | **0** |
| causal-bound MISMATCH | 0 | 0 |

**Three results, all reproducible across both runs:**

1. **Every corrupted item is a PREFILL item; not one of the 896 decode-row items is ever wrong.**
   In repeat 1 that is ALL 56 prefill items (8 q tiles x 7 kv heads) and nothing else.
2. **Uniform across `q_tile` AND `kv_head`.** This independently confirms the retraction above:
   there is no `q_start` dependence whatsoever -- the earlier "q tiles 1 and 2" was purely my
   lowest-16 sampling.
3. **The causal bound matches the reference for every item**, so that suspect stays dead.

**The distinguishing property is `qo_len`.** A prefill item owns a **full 128-packed-row q tile**
(all 8 MMA warps carry real rows); a decode item owns **4 packed rows** (one partially-filled warp,
seven idle). Combined with the warp-quantised damage (runs of exactly 16 packed rows), the defect
lives in the **multi-row q-tile path** and cannot express itself on a 4-row tile.

**And this REVERSES the victim/aggressor assumption I had been carrying.** The threshold sweep showed
bad rows growing with `DEC_ROWS`, which I read as "more items per CTA -> more corruption". But the
decode items are themselves CLEAN. So adding decode rows does not add corrupted decode output -- it
adds **damage to the prefill tiles**. The decode items are the **aggressor**; the prefill item is the
**victim**.

**The constraint that makes this sharp:** `KVPERREQ=1` passes, so the bad data is request 0's **own**
KV, not a decode request's. Therefore *a decode item's execution causes the prefill item to re-read a
WRONG TILE OF ITS OWN REQUEST* -- the decode item leaves state (pipeline stage, smem, or scheduler)
that makes the next prefill tile index wrongly, without ever importing decode data.

**Next, and it is now a narrow question:** what does a 4-packed-row decode item leave behind that a
128-row item does not? Candidates, all per-item and all checkable: the pipeline stage count it
advances (`num_kv_tiles` for kv=2048 is the same 15-16, so it consumes a FULL tile sequence for 4
rows of output); the `q_tile_idx * CTA_Q >= qo_len` early-`continue` path, which a decode item with
`qo_len=4` packed can hit where a prefill item cannot; and the epilogue's partial-tile store. The
early-continue path is the leading candidate because it is the one place an item exits the loop
WITHOUT running the pipeline to completion -- and the doc's own comment says both `continue` paths
"skip it on BOTH sides symmetrically", an invariant that has never been tested.

**[!!] RETRACTED -- "DETERMINISTIC IN `q_start`" WAS AN ARTIFACT OF MY OWN SAMPLING
(2026-10-10).** The heading below read *"BREAKTHROUGH: the corruption is deterministic in `q_start`
-- q tiles 1 and 2 of 8 are wrong in every block"*. **It is not.** Three compounding errors, all
mine:

1. **I sampled the 16 LOWEST bad row indices** (`_badset[:16]`). Low rows live in low q tiles, so
   the culprit list was *guaranteed* to come out as the first two or three q tiles whatever the
   truth. The "pattern" was my slice.
2. **The next run contradicted it directly:** culprits came back as q tiles **0 and 1** (items
   0,1,8,9,16,17,...) where the first run gave tiles **1 and 2** (items 1,2,9,10,...). A
   deterministic `q_start` dependence cannot move between runs.
3. **My retraction of the "unsplit" claim was ALSO wrong.** Every item reports `kv=[0,2048)`,
   `ckv=2048` -- they ARE unsplit. The 952 items decompose exactly as
   **8 q tiles x 7 kv heads = 56** (prefill) **+ 128 decode rows x 7 kv heads = 896** = 952. I had
   forgotten the `kv_head` dimension and inferred chunking from the item count, so item index
   encodes `(q_tile = i % 8, kv_head = i // 8)`.

**What the run DID establish, and it is solid:** `kern_limit == ref_limit` for **every** item, so
the chunk-relative causal bound is **correct** -- and since the items are unsplit, the earlier
unsplit arithmetic check covers them properly after all. Both causal-bound suspects are therefore
genuinely exonerated; it is the q-tile *localisation* that evaporates, not that result.

**Sampling fixed:** the decode now maps ALL bad rows and reports the DISTRIBUTION over
`(q_tile, kv_head)` rather than listing a biased prefix. Until that runs, the only honest statement
about which items are corrupted is: **unknown**.

**Lesson worth keeping, because it nearly became a published finding:** a "pattern" seen only in the
lowest-indexed members of a sample is a property of the sample. Two of today's strongest-looking
results -- this one and the tile-sequence trace aimed at block 0 -- were artifacts of looking only
where it was cheap to look.



```
verdict: bad rows 84/384                  <- host-side only, so the arm STILL FAILS
work_indptr[:12] = [0, 7, 14, 21, 28, 36, 43, 50, 57, 64, 72, 79]   total_items=952
bad rows map to task-3 items: [1, 2, 9, 10, 17, 18, 25, 26, 33, 34]
```

Each block owns ~7 items with `q_start` drawn from `{0,128,256,384,512,640,768,896}`, and the bad
items are **exactly the `q_start=128` and `q_start=256` ones, in EVERY block**:

| block | bad items | their `q_start` | clean siblings' `q_start` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1, 2 | **128, 256** | 0, 384, 512, 640, 768 |
| 1 | 9, 10 | **128, 256** | 896, 0, 384, 512 |
| 2 | 17, 18 | **128, 256** | ... |
| 3 | 25, 26 | **128, 256** | ... |
| 4 | 33, 34 | **128, 256** | ... |

**The plan data is CORRECT.** Culprits and clean siblings carry identical `batch=0` and
`kv_len=2048`; the only thing distinguishing them is `q_start`. So the planner is exonerated and the
fault is **q-tile-selective**: q tiles 1 and 2 of 8 are always wrong, everywhere, while tiles 0 and
3-7 are always right.

**This is Effect 1 made visible.** The two-effect model predicted a deterministic wrong-tile fault
plus a timing-dependent amplifier, and that is exactly what the data shows: the SET of corrupted
items is fixed and structural (`q_start` 128 and 256), while the COUNT of bad rows varies run to run
(84 here, 124 earlier, 96-128 across the determinism sweep) because Effect 2 modulates how much of
each affected tile is spoiled.

**Why this is the most actionable result in the investigation:** `q_start` feeds the causal bound.
For a 256-token request with `kv_len=2048`, token `t` may attend keys up to `kv_total - qo_len + t`
= `1792 + t`, so each q tile has its own kv-tile count, and tiles 1 and 2 are precisely where that
count transitions. The suspects are now narrow and all arithmetic:

* `get_num_kv_tiles`'s packed-GQA bound -- `last_tok = ((q_tile_idx + 1) * CTA_Q - 1) / g_pk` and
  `ceil_div(last_tok + 1 + ckv - qo_len / g_pk, CTA_KV)` -- evaluated at `q_tile_idx` 1 and 2;
* `col_limit_right`'s `(qo_idx / gqa_g) + 1 + ckv - qo_len_tok` at the same tiles;
* the split-KV `causal_kv_len` shift, since these items are chunked.

All three are per-q-tile arithmetic, all three were ported by hand, and all three are checkable on
the HOST by evaluating the same formulae for `q_tile_idx` 0..7 and comparing against the causal
reference's own per-tile key counts -- no GPU run and no device instrumentation.

**[!] MY OWN PROPOSED MECHANISM IS ALREADY PROTECTED -- refuted before building the fix I
announced (2026-10-10). Twenty-second elimination.**

Last entry proposed: *"the `consumer_wait` -> gemm -> `consumer_release` sequence is per-warpgroup,
not per-warp, so a warp that passes `WarpScheduler::barrier_sync()` and issues its gemm before its
peers can read a stage the pipeline considers released."* Checked the code before spending a build
cycle on it. **It cannot happen, for two independent reasons:**

1. **`pipeline_params.consumer_arv_count = NUM_MMA_THREADS`** (`prefill_sm90.cuh:120`). A stage is
   not released until **every** MMA thread has called `consumer_release`, so no single warp can
   release a stage out from under its peers. The arrival count is the protection, and it is already
   set to the full consumer width.
2. **`warpgroup_wait<1>()` precedes every `consumer_release`** (`mainloop_mma.cuh:244-245`,
   and the same pattern in each loop). The gemm has drained before the release, so a warp cannot
   still be reading the stage it releases.

So the per-warp *release* story is dead. Recorded as an elimination of my own proposal rather than
quietly dropped -- and the build cycle it would have cost was saved by reading first, which is the
same discipline that killed the tile-count and scheduler-desync candidates earlier today.

**What this does NOT touch:** the per-warp **granularity** is a measurement (runs of exactly 16
packed rows, warps 1/4/5 in one run) and stands. The corruption is still warp-quantised; what is
refuted is one specific explanation of how a warp could end up with the wrong K.

**Remaining live space, honestly bounded.** Twenty-two eliminations, and every synchronisation
mechanism reachable by reading is verified correct: arrival counts, tile counts, stage indices,
cp.async coverage, scheduler determinism, acquire/release pairing, lane mapping, gather addressing,
parity uniformity, warp-release ordering. The defect is a race, within one item, wrong KV tile of the
item's own request, warp-quantised, 4x depth-scaled, invisible to in-kernel instruments. **I have no
remaining candidate that is both consistent with all of that and checkable by reading.** The next
step that is not a guess is the `(block, work_idx)` plan-entry comparison from the fixed host decode
-- comparing a corrupted item's own plan data (`q_start`, `kv_start`, `kv_end`, `kv_len`,
`partial_indptr`) against its clean neighbours, since per-item plan data is the only input that
differs between items in the same block.

**[x] THE CORRUPTION UNIT IS A WHOLE MMA WARP, AND IT IS NOT A FIXED WARP (2026-10-10). Derived
from the already-captured `BADROWS` -- no new GPU run.**

Packed row = `token*G + head` with G=4, and MMA warp *w* owns packed rows `16w .. 16w+15`:

| bad token rows | packed rows | warp |
|---|---|---|
| 4, 5, 6, 7 | 16 .. 31 | **1** |
| 16, 17, 18, 19 | 64 .. 79 | **4** |
| 20, 21, 22, 23 | 80 .. 95 | **5** |

Every run is **exactly 4 token rows = 16 packed rows = one warp's share**, verified
programmatically, and the affected warps are **1, 4 and 5** -- several warps in a single run, not
one.

Three things follow, and the second rules out a whole class:

1. **The corruption unit is a whole MMA warp's output.** Granularity confirmed independently of the
   `NB_SYNC` arm.
2. **It is NOT a fixed warp.** A statically miswired warp (wrong accumulator offset, wrong row
   mapping) would hit the SAME warp index every time. Warps 1, 4, 5 in one run kills that class --
   which is also why the defect is a race and not an addressing constant.
3. **The fault happens WITHIN one item.** All these rows lie inside the FIRST q tile of request 0
   (`token rows 0..31` = `packed 0..127` = one CTA_Q tile), so whatever goes wrong does so while a
   single work item is being processed, not across an item boundary. That is a meaningful narrowing:
   the cross-item framing was about which TILE is loaded, but the damage is contained in one tile's
   warps.

**Combined picture now:** a race, inside one work item, that corrupts an arbitrary subset of that
tile's eight MMA warps, each all-or-nothing, with the wrong data being a different KV tile of the
same request, scaling 4x with pipeline depth, and invisible to any in-kernel instrument.

**Next, and it follows directly:** eight warps share `smem_k`/`smem_v` stages but each holds its own
accumulator and its own `tSrQ` descriptor. A subset of warps reading a stage while the producer
refills it would corrupt exactly those warps' rows. The `consumer_wait` -> gemm -> `consumer_release`
sequence is per-warpgroup, not per-warp, so a warp that passes `WarpScheduler::barrier_sync()` and
issues its gemm before its peers can read a stage the pipeline considers released. Testing that means
making the release wait for ALL warps, not just the warpgroup leader -- which `FUSED_O_HANDSHAKE`
does for `sO` and nothing currently does for `smem_k`/`smem_v`.

**[~] PER-WARP HYPOTHESIS: the `NB_SYNC` override is NOT the route; warp ordering NOT fully
exonerated (2026-10-10). Twentieth elimination, with the limit stated in advance.**

The granularity clue gave the hypothesis: bad rows arrive in aligned runs of 4 token rows = **16
packed rows**, and with CTA_Q=128 over 8 MMA warps, 16 packed rows is **exactly one warp's share of
the output**. So one warp's QK gemm using a different K tile than its peers would produce precisely
this, and it satisfies all five measured constraints (race, wrong tile, same request, >1 item/CTA,
4x depth scaling). `FUSED_NB_SYNC` gates the `WarpScheduler::barrier_sync`/`barrier_arrive`
overrides that order MMA warps around each gemm.

| arm | fails | bad rows of 384 |
|---|---|---|
| `NB_SYNC=1` (default) | 6/6 | 96, 112, 128, 116, 100, 88 -- mean ~107 |
| `NB_SYNC=0` (override off) | 6/6 | 104, 88, 72, 92, 112, 108 -- mean ~96 |

Ranges overlap heavily; no meaningful change. **Stated before the arm ran and still binding:** a
no-change does NOT exonerate warp ordering, because both settings may order warps adequately while
something else diverges. What it does establish is that this knob is not the fix.

**The per-warp GRANULARITY remains the strongest live clue** -- it is a measurement, not a
hypothesis, and it survives this arm untouched. The next step that uses it properly is the
`(block, work_idx)` mapping from the now-fixed host decode (byte offsets / 4): take a specific bad
run of 4 token rows, identify the item and block that own it, and read that item's plan entries
(`q_start`, `kv_start`, `kv_end`, `kv_len`, `partial_indptr`) against its neighbours. If one warp's
16 rows are wrong, the item's own plan data is the only per-item input that could differ.

BADROWS [(4, 5.59), (5, 5.17), (6, 5.64), (7, 5.02),

**The validity check is the important part of the first line.** Every device-side route to this

**NEW STRUCTURAL CLUE, the first thing learned about WHICH rows are wrong:** bad rows come in
**aligned runs of 4 consecutive token rows** (4-7, 16-19, 20-23, ...). At G=4 that is **16 packed
rows** per run -- and 16 is exactly `size(dst)` and `NUM_KV_PER_ITER` from the `[kvinv-dims]`
output. So the corruption granularity is **one gather iteration**, not one tile (128 packed rows /
32 token rows) and not one item. Whatever goes wrong spoils the 16 packed rows a thread group
handles in a single pass, which is a much tighter target than "a tile".

**And a bug in my own decode, fixed:** `work_indptr` came back all zeros because I read the plan's
`*_offset` fields as int32 INDICES. They are **BYTE** offsets -- the stride between consecutive
field offsets is 3808 bytes = **952 int32s**, and 952 is exactly the item count, which is what
identified the units. Dividing by 4 is the fix; re-running.

**[!] CATCH-22: THE CORRELATION CANNOT BE DONE WITH DEVICE PRINTS AT ALL (2026-10-10).** Fixing
the aiming problem exposed a structural one.

```
verdict: bad rows 0/384        <- PASSED, so there was nothing to correlate
[item] lines: 952   [tile] lines: 216
bad rows mapped to 0 distinct (block, item) pairs
```

Adding the per-item identity print made the arm **pass**: 952 + 216 device prints serialise the
kernel and mask the race, exactly as documented for every other probe (printf 76/384 -> 0/384,
racecheck, memcheck 0 errors AND 0/384). So:

* correlating bad rows to items **requires** per-item identity from the device;
* device `printf` **masks the defect**;
* therefore **the race cannot be correlated by printing**. This is not a scripting mistake, it is
  the method being self-defeating, and it rules out the whole approach rather than one attempt.

**THE WAY OUT -- stop asking the device.** The item -> output-row mapping is a property of the
PLAN, which is built on the HOST by `FusedFourTaskPlan` before the kernel launches. `work_indptr`
gives each block's item range, and each item's `q_start` / `qo_indptr` / `q_tile_idx` /
`o_indices` give the output rows it owns. Decoding those arrays in the harness needs **zero device
code and therefore perturbs nothing**:

1. dump the plan tensors in `fused_reference.py` (they are already passed to
   `torch.ops.fused_fa3.fused_run`);
2. map every `BADROWS` index to its owning `(block, work_idx)` on the host;
3. only then, if a device trace is still needed, gate it to that single `(block, work_idx)` so the
   print volume is ~2 lines instead of 1168 -- small enough that it may not mask.

Step 3's viability is itself an open question: even a handful of prints may perturb enough. The
honest fallback is the register-accumulate pattern -- have the kernel WRITE the per-item tile
sequence to a global buffer (plain stores, not `printf`) which the host reads after the launch.
Global stores are what the kernel already does for output; they do not serialise like `printf`,
and the per-item accounting instrument already proved that writing-then-reporting preserves the
defect (124/384 with it enabled).

**Standing method rule this adds, worth keeping:** on this defect, ANY instrument that emits from
inside the kernel while the race is live destroys the measurement. Only two patterns have survived:
(a) register accumulation reported after the loop, and (b) a check of a DETERMINISTIC property,
where serialisation is irrelevant. Future instruments must be one of those two.

instead of the item's. Stating expectations in advance is only worth anything if they are derived
from the right quantity.

**And the test was aimed at the wrong place.** I traced `blockIdx.x == 0`, but at dec=8 there is
exactly **1 bad row of 264**, which may belong to any of the 132 blocks. So "block 0's sequence is
correct" says nothing about the block that actually corrupts. This neither confirms nor refutes
Effect 1; it is a null measurement with a wrongly-chosen target, and it is recorded as such rather
than as evidence that the gather is sound.

   scaling. The `sO`/`smem_v` union is already measured as a real DEPTH-DEPENDENT contributor
   (~29% at 2 stages, nothing at 1) and fits this slot exactly.

**This dissolves the tension recorded in `0e3bb0496`**, where I noted that a wrong-tile logic error
should be deterministic while the defect is not, and listed it as unresolved. The resolution is that
no single mechanism has to be both: there are two, and the seventeen eliminations were searching for
one thing that explained everything.

**NEXT, and it is now a well-posed question rather than a hunt:** is the deterministic sequence
CORRECT? Compare the per-block signature against the sequence the PLAN says that block's items

offending item and tile directly. This is the first step in this investigation that compares against
an independently-derived expectation rather than against another arm of the kernel.

**[x] SHUFFLE-LANE INVARIANT HOLDS -- seventeenth elimination, and it kills BOTH shuffle-site

Ran the `[kvinv]` probe that had sat in the tree unused (`FLASHINFER_FA3_PARTIAL_PROBE`,
`sparse_mainloop.cuh:400`) with its expected output written down in advance. **Why printf masking
does not apply here:** the invariant `kv_offset % KV_STRIDE == group_id` is DETERMINISTIC
arithmetic, not the race, so serialising the kernel cannot hide a violation -- unlike every earlier
probe, where serialisation destroyed the signal.

```
[kvinv-dims] CTA_KV=128 NUM_KV_PER_ITER=16 KV_STRIDE=8 NUM_GROUPS=8

nonzero bad counts:  (none)
[kvinv-bad] VIOLATIONS: 0
```

1. **The lane mapping is correct.** `src_thread = group_id*THREADS_PER_GROUP + kv_offset/KV_STRIDE`
   fetches the intended lane's offset for every `(thread, i)` pair checked.
2. **The "silent page 0" path is also dead**, and the dims prove it: `NUM_ITERS_PER_GROUP = 16`
   equals `THREADS_PER_GROUP = 16`, so `thread_in_group < NUM_ITERS_PER_GROUP` is ALWAYS true and
   `k = kv_offset/8 < 16` always holds. The `else my_kv_offset[parity] = 0` branch can therefore
   fire only through the `kv_len` predicate -- where the reader's `guard` matches the source lane's
   validity exactly, so no reader consumes a zeroed offset.

(The arm's own verdict was 0/264 because `FA3_PROBE=1` serialises and masks the RACE, exactly as
documented. That does not bear on the invariant, which is why this probe is usable and the others
were not.)

**So of the two suspects named in the previous entry, both are gone.** What remains is the `parity`
double-buffer itself -- case 1 (timing-dependent divergence) or case 3 (parity fine, wrong tile
arrives another way) from the pre-registered list -- and the experiment that separates them is
already specified there: per-thread `(kv_tile_idx, parity)` signatures accumulated in registers and
printed after the loop.

**[>] THE PARITY MECHANISM, AND AN UNRESOLVED TENSION WITH IT (2026-10-10). Next step, stated
before running anything so it cannot be fitted to a result.**

**Mechanism.** `__shfl_sync(FULL_MASK, my_kv_offset[parity], src_thread)` (`sparse_mainloop.cuh:440`):
each thread evaluates `my_kv_offset[parity]` with **its own** `parity`, and the shuffle returns the
value *src_thread* computed. If `src_thread`'s parity differs from the reader's, the reader receives
**the other buffer slot** -- a different TILE of the same request, which is exactly the measured
signature. `parity` is a thread-local `int` (line 341) toggled at **seven** hand-managed sites
(651, 662, 672, 681, 692, 702) with comments tracking `parity=0/1` through interleaved K and V
paths. That is precisely the shape of state machine where one path through the loop leaves the
value inconsistent.

**Unresolved tension, recorded rather than smoothed over.** A wrong-tile *logic* error would be
**DETERMINISTIC**, but the defect is **nondeterministic** (same build, same seed: 96 100 88 88 92
84). Three possibilities, and they are distinguishable:

1. `parity` DIVERGES across threads only under some timing-dependent path, so the shuffle slot is
   race-dependent. Would explain both the wrong tile and the variance.
2. The wrong-tile write is deterministic and a SECOND, timing-dependent effect modulates how many
   output rows it spoils. Two effects, which the ~4x depth scaling would then be shared between.
3. `parity` is uniform and correct, and the wrong tile arrives some other way -- in which case the
   tile localisation stands but the parity suspect is wrong.

**How to separate them without guessing:** the register-counting pattern already proven not to mask
the defect. Per thread, accumulate a signature of the `(kv_tile_idx, parity)` pairs it actually
gathered -- e.g. `sig ^= (kv_tile_idx * 2 + parity) * (i + 1)` -- and print per block after the
loop. If threads within a warp report different signatures for the same item, case 1 is confirmed
and names the diverging site; if every thread agrees yet the tile is still wrong, case 3. A
deterministic signature across repeats with varying bad-row counts is case 2.

**Why `parity` uniformity is NOT yet established by reading:** every toggle sits inside a branch on
`kv_tile_idx`, which is uniform across the warpgroup, so uniformity is *plausible* -- but
`prefetch_kv_offset`'s `valid_read` is thread-dependent (`thread_in_group < NUM_ITERS_PER_GROUP`),
and threads failing it write `my_kv_offset[parity] = 0`. A zero offset is a VALID-LOOKING page
offset, so a reader shuffling from such a lane gets page 0 of the cache rather than a guard
violation. That is worth checking directly: it would corrupt with no divergence in `parity` at all.

**[x] POSITIVELY LOCALISED: THE WRONG KV *TILE* IS LOADED -- row/lane addressing exonerated
(2026-10-10). Sixteenth elimination and the best-aimed state this investigation has reached.**

`KVPERTILE=1` makes pages identical **within each `CTA_KV` tile** and distinct **across** tiles,
aligned to the same boundaries the kernel tiles on (`FA3_CTA_KV`, read from the env so it cannot
drift). dec=128, `STAGES=2`, baseline, warm dir, 6 seeds:

| arm | fails | bad rows of 384 |
|---|---|---|
| control, all pages distinct | 6/6 | 100, 104, 116, 112, 96, 124 -- mean ~109 |
| **identical within tile, distinct across** | **6/6** | 120, 112, 104, 104, 120, 112 -- mean ~112 |

**Unchanged.** Identical rows inside a tile would have HIDDEN any wrong-row-within-tile error; it
hid nothing. So:

* **row/lane addressing is EXONERATED** -- the `__shfl_sync(FULL_MASK, my_kv_offset[parity],
  src_thread)` mapping and the `kv_offset` arithmetic are fine. This agrees with the hand-check:
  `src_thread = group_id * THREADS_PER_GROUP + kv_offset / KV_STRIDE` with `THREADS_PER_GROUP = 16`
  and `k < 16` always lands in the caller's own warp, so the implicit `%32` resolves to the
  intended thread.
* **the TILE INDEX is what is wrong.** The consumer/producer is working on a different kv tile of
  its own request.

**The surviving suspect is `my_kv_offset[parity]`, the 2-entry rolling buffer** (`sparse_mainloop.cuh:339`,
toggled `parity ^= 1`). A wrong parity loads a different TILE of the same request -- precisely the
measured signature. It is also the only single candidate that explains the **4x pipeline-depth
scaling** on its own, and it is a race by construction: the parity toggles across the
prefetch/consume handoff, so producer and consumer can disagree about which slot holds the tile
currently being loaded.

**Full constraint set, every item measured, and the parity buffer satisfies all five:** a race;
wrong kv TILE; of the item's OWN request; requires >1 work item per CTA; magnitude scales ~4x with
pipeline depth.

**Next:** read the parity toggle against the prefetch/consume order in `load()` -- `prefetch_kv_offset`
writes `my_kv_offset[parity]`, `load_kv_with_gather` reads it, and the K and V paths interleave
with their own toggles at lines 641-711. A toggle that happens between a tile's prefetch and its
gather, or a K path that toggles while the V path still needs the old slot, produces exactly this.

**[!!] RETRACTION, AND IT INVERTS THE LOCALISATION: THE WRONG ROWS ARE *WITHIN* THE SAME
REQUEST, NOT FROM ANOTHER ONE (2026-10-10).**

I read the `KVPERREQ` discriminator backwards and then repeated the error in five commits
(`683dc9141`, `09cc03410`, `776c924c0`, `c0462732a`, `664d758b2`). The correct derivation:

`KVPERREQ=1` makes pages identical **within** a request and distinct **across** requests. So

* a read of the wrong row **inside the same request** returns the **RIGHT** value -> **invisible**;
* a read from **another request** returns a wrong value -> **VISIBLE**.

That arm **PASSED 0/8**. A cross-request read would have FAILED it. Therefore:

| arm | result | what it proves |
|---|---|---|
| all pages identical (`KVCONST=1`) | PASS 0/8 | any wrong-row read is invisible |
| identical within request (`KVPERREQ=1`) | **PASS 0/8** | **NO cross-request reads** |
| all pages distinct (control) | FAIL 8/8 | wrong-row reads **WITHIN** the request |

**The defect is the consumer reducing the WRONG KV ROWS OF ITS OWN REQUEST.** Every statement in
this doc and CHANGELOG of the form "CTAs read another request's K/V" is **WRONG** and is retracted;
what the data supports is "CTAs read the wrong kv rows, and those rows belong to the same request".

**What survives untouched:** it is a race (within-build repeats vary on both seeds); it needs >1
work item per CTA; it scales ~4x with pipeline depth; it is invisible to every serialising
instrument but not to register counting; all fifteen structural eliminations (none of them depended
on the cross-request reading); and both confirmed contributors with their depth-scoping.

**What this REDIRECTS:** a wrong row within the request means a wrong INDEX, not stale foreign
data -- so the suspect list is now the gather's own addressing arithmetic, which I had set aside
precisely because I believed the data came from elsewhere:

* `__shfl_sync(FULL_MASK, my_kv_offset[parity], src_thread)` -- picks **another lane's** page
  offset, i.e. another ROW OF THE SAME REQUEST, which is exactly the corrected signature. Any lane
  divergence at that shuffle makes the result undefined.
* `my_kv_offset[parity]` -- the 2-entry rolling buffer. A wrong `parity` loads a different TILE of
  the same request.
* `kv_base_idx = kv_tile_idx * CTA_KV` combined with `kv_offset` from the coordinate tensor.

All three produce wrong-row-same-request, are data-dependent, and are depth-dependent through the
parity buffer. **This is a better-aimed space than anything the fifteen eliminations left**, and it
exists only because the earlier reading was wrong.

eliminated, and structural candidates are now EXHAUSTED (2026-10-10).**

dec=128, `STAGES=1`, 6 seeds, same build set:

|---|---|---|
| `SPLIT_SMEM_O=0` (control, `sO` aliases `smem_v`) | 6/6 | 16, 28, 20, 20, 12, 15 -- mean ~19 |
| `SPLIT_SMEM_O=1` (un-aliased) | **6/6** | 23, 16, 16, 20, 6, 16 -- mean ~16 |

**So the union only matters when the pipeline has depth**: at 2 stages the producer runs ahead and

**STRUCTURAL CANDIDATES ARE EXHAUSTED.** Fifteen eliminated; every synchronisation mechanism

pipeline stage with no `sO` aliasing**.

takes the FA3 role so FA2 should never write there, but anything that does would corrupt K/V stages
while leaving every count consistent -- exactly what is observed. Testable as one bit only at
`STAGES=1`, since disjoint does not fit at two stages.

**MECHANISM, read off the source and consistent with every prior measurement:**

* `load_tail` -- the pipeline drain -- is called **ONCE, after the whole persistent loop**
  (`prefill_sm90.cuh:285`), and `smem_pipe_write_k/v` and `smem_pipe_read_k/v` are declared
  **outside** the loop and carried across every item.
* So if the consumer consumes even one fewer stage than the producer loaded for some item, the
  pipeline **shifts permanently**, and from that item on every consumer reads a stage filled for a
  different request. Stock cannot hit this: with one item per CTA there is no next item to inherit
  the shift.
* It retro-explains the handshake result exactly: `FUSED_O_HANDSHAKE` rendezvoused both loops and
  **halved** corruption (112 -> 56) without fixing it, because a rendezvous realigns *timing* while
  leaving the stage **indices** shifted.
* It fits the items/CTA threshold (clean below 1 item/CTA, 15/15), the data dependence (causal tile
  counts vary per item), and the serialisation-masking (a producer kept slow never runs ahead).

**RULED OUT BY READING, before spending GPU time:**

* **Producer/consumer tile-count disagreement.** Both sites call the SAME `get_num_kv_tiles` with
  the SAME arguments including `fused_causal_kv_len(work_tile_info, kv_len)`
  (`prefill_sm90.cuh:247` and `:325`). They agree.
* **Scheduler desync.** `UnifiedWgmmaTileScheduler` is fully deterministic --
  `work_indptr[blockIdx.x]` slices per block and `counter` advances -- `get_next_work` ignores
  `is_producer`, and `prefetch_next_work`/`broadcast_next_work` are no-ops. Both warpgroups walk
  the identical item sequence, and both `continue` conditions evaluate identical data.

**NEXT, and it must be a measurement not a guess:** count tiles LOADED vs tiles CONSUMED per item
on both sides and compare. A per-item drain plus a pipeline-state reset is the obvious fix, but
resetting `PipelineState` without resetting the pipeline's own mbarrier phases is exactly the
bookkeeping that deadlocked the `barrier_O` attempt -- so the count comes first, then the fix is
aimed rather than attempted.

**A methodological correction that affects how these arms should be read.** `SEED` sets the input
data, not the race: the same seed gives different outcomes on different runs (seed 5 -> NOVERDICT
in the arm, 82 bad rows on retry). So one run per seed is fine as *sampling*, but a per-arm
NOVERDICT *rate* is a property of 10 random draws, not of the arm -- the apparent 3/10 vs 1/10
difference between the two arms carries no weight, and an earlier statement in this session that
"the fence introduces an intermittent hang" was wrong on exactly that basis and is retracted.

**[!] `barrier_O` CANNOT CARRY THE Q INVARIANT -- reusing it DEADLOCKS, and working out why
settled what that barrier actually means (2026-10-10).**

The first fence implementation moved `barrier_O`'s arrival to the end of the consumer's mma and
hoisted its wait above the Q load. It **compiled and then hung**: GPU pinned at **100% for 17
minutes** on a kernel that runs in microseconds (same signature as the earlier `FA3_MBARRIER`
hang). Killed rather than left to burn the 30-minute cap.

**Why, and this is the useful part.** The consumer's sequence is `mma(0), epi(0), mma(1),
epi(1), ...`, so an arrival at the START of `mma(N)` carries the meaning *"`epi(N-1)` is done"* --
which is exactly what licenses the producer to refill `smem_v`, the buffer `sO` **aliases**. So:

* **`barrier_O` is an `sO`/`smem_v` handshake**, not a Q handshake. It never protected `smem_q` --
  the Q load sits above it.
* Its arrival and wait are paired with an **offset of one work item**, and the arrival is guarded
  by `work_idx != 0`. Relocating the arrival left one wait with no matching arrival, which is the
  deadlock.
* Moving it would also have made things WORSE on the output side: the new arrival site sits
  **before** `epi(N-1)`, so the producer could refill `smem_v` while the epilogue was still
  reading `sO`. One barrier cannot carry both invariants.

That also explains why un-aliasing `sO` measured as a **separate** 45% contributor rather than a
duplicate of this one: two buffers, two invariants, one barrier.

**Reimplemented with a DEDICATED `barrier_Qdone`**, `barrier_O` left byte-identical to stock
(verified by diff on both files). One arrival per item, unconditional, from the mma warpgroup's
last warp after its final `sQ` read; the producer waits `(work_idx - 1) % 2` before refilling
`smem_q`, guarded at item 0 -- the same parity convention `barrier_Q` uses one line below, where
the k-th completion is awaited with parity `k % 2`. Arms now run under a short timeout so a
deadlock reports in minutes.

**[!] RETRACTION, in place: the first `FENCE=1` arm reported "fails 10/10" and that was an
ARTIFACT, not a result.** Two compounding mistakes, both mine:

1. **The patch did not compile.** The hoisted `barrier_O.wait` was inserted into
   `get_num_kv_tiles`, where neither `shared_storage` nor `work_idx` is in scope -- the insertion
   anchored on the first `#ifdef FLASHINFER_FUSED_PACKED_Q` in the file, which is in a different
   function from the one holding the wait. Re-patched to the top of `load()`, after the
   `block_coord` destructuring, which is above every write to `smem_q`.
2. **The harness scored a missing verdict as a failure.** `v=${t#bad rows }` yields an empty
   string when the run produces no verdict line at all, and `[ "$v" != "0" ]` is TRUE for the
   empty string -- so a build failure, a crash and a timeout all counted as "bad rows". The
   corrected script checks the build explicitly first, reports `NOVERDICT` separately from a
   numeric bad-row count, and refuses to continue if the build did not produce one.

This is the same family as the NaN gate recorded earlier in this doc -- a comparison that cannot
distinguish "measured nothing" from "measured zero". The fence hypothesis itself is **untested**;
the re-run is in flight.

**[!] MECHANISM, READ OFF THE SOURCE: the `smem_q` refill for item N+1 is unfenced against item
N's consumer.** Two premises, both verified by reading rather than inferred:

1. **The producer refills `smem_q` BEFORE it waits** (`sparse_mainloop.cuh`): the Q load is
   issued, and only then comes `barrier_O.wait((work_idx + 1) % 2)`. So nothing stands between
   the refill and the previous item's reader.
2. **The consumer signals `barrier_O` after only the FIRST QK gemm is ISSUED**
   (`mainloop_mma.cuh`, `wg_wait=-1`, guarded by `work_idx != 0`) -- and
   **`TiledMmaQK` is `GMMA::ss_op_selector`** (`kernel_traits.cuh:97`), i.e. BOTH operands come
   from shared memory, so `tSrQ` is a smem `DescriptorIterator` and `sQ` is re-read by every
   later kv tile's gemm, not consumed once into registers.

The only cross-item fence is therefore placed too late on the producer side and raised too early
on the consumer side. **This is stock 0.7 code**, sound for a CTA that runs one work item and a
hazard for one that runs many -- which is what our persistent scheduler creates and what the
sweep above measures. It predicts, without fitting:

* stock-configured arms failing too, at a lower rate (measured: mean 5.6 of 384 versus 128), since
  our 32-lane cp.async packed-Q load is in flight far longer than stock's TMA and widens the window;
* every serializing instrument hiding it (measured: printf probe 0/384 vs 76/384, racecheck
  indiscriminate, memcheck 0 errors and 0/384);
* it being in the SAME class as the one contributor already confirmed -- `sO`/`smem_v`, 45% -- which
  is the same bug on the output buffer instead of the input one.

`FUSED_Q_REUSE_FENCE=1` (loader knob `Q_REUSE_FENCE`) hoists the producer's wait above the Q load
and moves the consumer's arrival to after its last `sQ` read. It is expected to COST time: it
serializes producer and consumer across items. Correctness first; the A/B measures both.

**[x] MEMCHECK: 0 ERRORS -- no out-of-bounds access, so it is a pure ORDERING problem on in-bounds
shared memory.** `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` on the failing shape (`DEC_ROWS=128`,
`MIX_ALL_FA3=1`, the arm that fails 10/10 at mean ~128 bad rows):

```
ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors
mode=mix_decode worst rel err 0.002127, bad rows 0/384
```

Two things from that: **no invalid shared/global/local access anywhere**, and the run **passed
under the sanitizer** -- the slowdown masks it, exactly as `FA3_PROBE=1`'s printf did. Both
confirm timing-dependence and rule out the whole out-of-bounds class.

**Instrument status is now complete and unhelpful:** `racecheck` cannot discriminate (it flags
stock's own correct kernel), `memcheck` is clean, and any instrument slow enough to observe the
kernel makes the bug disappear. There is no tool left that will name this directly.

**Standing tally on this defect: nine hypotheses eliminated, one contributor confirmed.**
Eliminated: `kQueryEmpty` symmetry, `work_idx` symmetry, Q-completion mechanism, scheduler advance
logic, the store-completion handshake (made a clean arm dirty), same-output-row collisions,
per-request plan arrays, `(batch, q_start)` group crossings, and out-of-bounds access. Confirmed:
`sO`/`smem_v` aliasing, ~45% of the corruption (`FUSED_SPLIT_SMEM_O=1`).

**What is left is bisection by deletion, not by hypothesis.** The remaining ~55% is an ordering
problem among in-bounds shared buffers reused across work items, and the only approach not yet
tried is to remove capability until it goes clean: e.g. force `work_indptr` to one item per CTA and
accept dropping work (correctness-only arm, no timing meaning) to confirm the reuse class
end-to-end; then re-add items one at a time. That is slow but it terminates, which nine hypotheses
have not.

**It does not change the recommendation below.** A correct kernel here is still net-negative on
realistic batches, still under the 29% ceiling, and still slower than a baseline that already
fuses the batch into one kernel.

**[!] GROUP-CROSSING HYPOTHESIS REFUTED (2026-10-10) -- the eighth on this defect.** Implemented

outer), which makes a CTA's contiguous run share `(batch, q_start)` and differ only in kv chunk, at
identical total work. `MODE=mix_decode DEC_ROWS=128 MIX_ALL_FA3=1`, 3 runs each:

| arm | bad rows / 384 |
|---|---|
| default order (control) | 84, 80, 120 |
| **group-major** | **100, 96, 96** |
| group-major + `SPLIT_SMEM_O=1` | 83, 95, NON-FINITE |

**No improvement -- marginally worse.** So `sQ` being refilled with a different Q tile between
items is NOT the mechanism, and the neat explanation for the 217-items-passes anomaly is wrong. The
anomaly remains unexplained.

**Running tally on this one defect: eight refuted hypotheses** -- `kQueryEmpty` symmetry, `work_idx`
symmetry, the Q-completion mechanism, scheduler advance logic, the store-completion handshake
(which made a clean arm dirty), same-output-row collisions, per-request plan arrays, and now group
crossings. **One contributor found and quantified:** `sO`/`smem_v` aliasing, worth ~45%
(`FUSED_SPLIT_SMEM_O`).

**What I would do next, and why I am not continuing this way.** The one instrument not yet tried is
`compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` -- out-of-bounds shared or global access, which `racecheck` does
not cover and which would explain corruption with no race at all. That is a single run and it is
the honest next step. But eight refutations against one confirmed contributor is a poor rate, and
the strategic picture argues against spending more here regardless of the outcome:

- the fusion is **net-negative** on realistic 4-mode batches (1.46-2.01x slower than all-FA3), so
  fixing this race yields a *correct kernel that is still the wrong design*;
- B1's measured ceiling is **29%**, below the >=30% bar, so the kernel route cannot clear it alone;
- the baseline (`BatchAttention`) already does the whole batch in **one validated-correct persistent
  kernel** and is 1.11x-4.9x faster than ours everywhere.

**Recommendation, recorded for the decision it needs:** park the two-role fusion, and restate the
project on **FA3-only colocation** -- one kernel, linear in KV, no `sm_split` parameter, no
cross-role reuse, and already faster than the fusion on every realistic shape measured. Points 1,
2 and 4 of the PD-colocation argument do not depend on the fusion at all; point 3 is *stronger*
without it (see the 2026-10-10 section in `pd_colocation_vs_disagg.md`). That path has a live
chance at the bar; this one has three independent blockers.

**[REFUTED] A HYPOTHESIS THAT EXPLAINS EVERY OBSERVATION INCLUDING THE ANOMALY (2026-10-10): the defect
fires when a CTA's run CROSSES `(batch, q_start)` GROUP BOUNDARIES, i.e. when `sQ` must be refilled
with DIFFERENT Q data between items.**

The anomaly that needed explaining: **1 request at ~217 items/CTA PASSED** (qo=2048) while
**97 requests at ~5.5 items/CTA FAILED** (1 bad row). Items-per-CTA alone cannot produce that
ordering, so reuse *count* is not the variable.

What distinguishes them is **what the consecutive items are**:
- **One request:** a CTA's contiguous run `[ptr_begin, ptr_end)` is mostly items of the *same*
  `(batch, q_start)` group -- consecutive kv chunks of one q tile. Same `q_start` means the **same Q
  tile**, so `sQ` holds the same data across those items and is never refilled with different
  content. 217 such items in a row are harmless.
- **Many requests:** a run crosses group boundaries constantly, so `sQ` must be refilled with a
  different Q tile between items. 5.5 items/CTA spanning several groups is more dangerous than 217
  items within one.

**This fits every data point collected:**

| fixture | run composition | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 request, qo=2048, ~217 items/CTA | nearly all same-group | **PASS 0/2048** |
| 1 request, qo=4096, ~434 items/CTA | crosses a few group boundaries | 1 bad row / 4096 |
| 41 requests, 2.5 items/CTA | few crossings | PASS |
| 97 requests, 5.5 items/CTA | more crossings | 1 bad row |
| 129 requests, 7.2 items/CTA | crossings almost every item | 76-144 / 384 |

It also explains why un-aliasing `smem_o` removed only ~45%: that fixed the **`sO`** half of the
reuse hazard and left the **`sQ`** half, which is the one that tracks group crossings.

**The decisive test, and it is cheap:** hold items/CTA fixed and vary only the number of GROUP
CROSSINGS per run. The planner's `work_indptr` hands out items in plan order, and
`EnumerateFusedWorkItems` emits `for kv0 { for h { for q0 } } }` -- so **chunk is the OUTER loop**,
meaning consecutive items differ in `q0`/`h` and only rarely share a `q_start`. Reordering the
enumeration to `for h { for q0 { for kv0 } } }` would make consecutive items share `(batch,
q_start)` and differ only in chunk -- maximising same-group runs at identical total work. If the
corruption largely vanishes under that reordering, the `sQ`-refill-between-items mechanism is
confirmed, and the reordering is itself a candidate mitigation (it also improves `sQ` reuse, so it
may be a perf win independently).

**[~] UN-ALIASED `smem_o` FROM `smem_v` (`FUSED_SPLIT_SMEM_O=1`): a real 45% reduction, still not
a fix.** Stock unions them to save shared memory, which is safe for one work item per CTA. Our
persistent scheduler gives a CTA many, so the producer's V load for item N+1 can overwrite the `sO`
the epilogue is still reading for item N. Splitting them removes that hazard outright rather than
ordering around it:

| arm | FINAL smem | result |
|---|---|---|
| `SPLIT_SMEM_O=0` (default), dec=32 | 163920 | PASS 0/288 |
| `SPLIT_SMEM_O=1`, dec=32 | **196688** (+32768 = exactly `CTA_Q*HEAD_DIM_VO*2`) | PASS 0/288 |
| `SPLIT_SMEM_O=1`, dec=128, 5 runs | — | 73, 60, **NON-FINITE**, 55, 90 bad rows |

**Mean bad rows at dec=128: ~128 (aliased) -> ~70 (split), a ~45% reduction.** So the aliasing was
a genuine contributor and the hazard class is confirmed. It costs exactly the predicted 32 KB and
launches with headroom (196688 of 232448). **But it is not the whole cause** -- which is what the
four-corner bisect already implied (>=3 contributors), and one run still went non-finite.

**What remains, and it is now a short list.** `smem_q` is its OWN buffer (not aliased), but it is
still **refilled per work item**, so the producer's Q gather for item N+1 can overwrite the `sQ`
the consumer is still using for item N's QK MMA. `kQueryEmpty` exists to prevent exactly that and
is byte-identical to stock -- but stock's own multi-item path is the `BatchPrefillPersistentTileScheduler`
configuration, and **it has not been established that any shipped flashinfer wrapper actually
exercises it**. If stock's persistent path is itself untested upstream, then `kQueryEmpty`'s
correctness under heavy reuse is an open question rather than a settled one.

**Left OFF by default**, same reasoning as the handshake: a flag that removes 45% of a correctness
bug makes the remainder rarer and harder to catch. It goes on when the set is complete.

**[x] SEPARATION DONE (2026-10-10): REQUEST COUNT IS NOT REQUIRED. The defect tracks WORK-ITEM
COUNT.** Two harness fixes were needed first:
1. **`ORACLE=ba`** -- use the validated `BatchAttention` as the correctness oracle where the fp32
   reference is unaffordable (it is O(qo x kv x heads) in Python). Validated against fp32 on a
   fixture both can run: fp32 0.003303 vs BA 0.004407, **both 0/1024**.
2. **`FWS` 1 GB -> 8 GB.** Everything past qo~2048 was failing with
   `FusedFourTaskPlan failed: invalid argument` -- the PLAN BUILDER, not the kernel. At
   qo=2048 / kv=8192 the planner picks a 128-wide kv chunk, giving 64 chunks x 64 q tiles, so
   `partial_o` alone needs **~939 MB** (524288 partial rows x 7 kv heads x 128 dims x 2 B). A
   harness limit that had been masquerading as a kernel ceiling for several sweeps.

With both fixed, **one request** at rising scale:

| fixture | `num_merge_rows` | items / CTA | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| qo=2048, kv=8192, **1 request** | 8192 | ~217 | **PASS 0/2048** |
| qo=4096, kv=8192, **1 request** | 16384 | ~434 | **1 bad row / 4096**, rel 0.2989 |

**So a SINGLE request corrupts at sufficient scale: request count is not necessary.** The defect
scales with the number of work items (and therefore with how many times a CTA reuses `sQ`/`sO`),
not with the number of requests. That **rules out the per-request plan arrays** -- the direction
several of the refuted hypotheses were circling -- and leaves cross-item reuse as the mechanism,
which is what the four-corner bisect also pointed to.

**[!] AND A SEPARATE FINDING worth recording on its own: the partial slab grows as
O(packed_qo x num_kv_chunks).** Nearly a gigabyte of partials for ONE 2048-token chunk at 8K
context, and 16384 merge rows at qo=4096. That is a real serving concern independent of
correctness -- at production context lengths the split-KV workspace alone would dominate the KV
cache budget. It also explains why the chunk-size sweep gave 4.5x: larger chunks cut this
quadratically.

**[SUPERSEDED] [~] SEPARATION ATTEMPTED, BLOCKED BY THE ORACLE.** In every sweep so far, request count and
items-per-CTA grew together (41 requests = 2.5 items/CTA passed; 129 = 7.2 failed), so neither was
isolated. One request with a long `qo` gives many items/CTA at request count 1:

| qo (1 request, kv=8192) | items | items/CTA | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | ~224 | ~1.7 | **PASS 0/1024** |
| 2048 | ~448 | ~3.4 | **NO OUTPUT** |
| 4096 | ~896 | ~6.8 | **NO OUTPUT** |

The two larger arms produce nothing: the fp32 causal reference is **O(qo x kv x heads)** in Python
and becomes unaffordable past qo~2048 at kv=8192 (it either OOMs or exceeds the 600 s cap). So the
separation cannot be done with this oracle -- the harness, not the kernel, is the limit.

**The fix is a cheaper oracle, and one is already validated: `BatchAttention`.** It passes the
fp32 reference at 0 bad rows on every fixture tested, so it can serve as the correctness oracle at
sizes where fp32 is unaffordable -- compare fused output against `BatchAttention` output rather
than against fp32. That makes the whole (requests x items-per-CTA) plane reachable and is a
prerequisite for separating these two variables at all.

**Revised next steps, in order:**
1. **Switch the oracle to `BatchAttention` for large fixtures** (keep fp32 for the small ones as the
   validation of the oracle itself). ~15 lines in the driver; it already runs `BatchAttention`.
2. Then rerun the separation: one request with qo 2048-16384 to get 3-30 items/CTA at request
   count 1. That settles whether the corruption tracks reuse or request count -- which the last
   seven hypotheses were all circling.
3. `--tool memcheck` for out-of-bounds smem/global access, which racecheck does not cover and which
   would explain corruption with no race at all.

**Not worth doing:** chasing the 17 racecheck hazards (it flags stock's correct kernel too), or more
inspection-led hypotheses -- seven have now been refuted, and the common factor is that none of them
was a measurement that could distinguish the two live variables.

**[SUPERSEDED] [x] FOUR-CORNER BISECT (2026-10-10), and it CORRECTS my "stock paths are CLEAN" claim.** Split
`write_packed`'s gate (`FUSED_PACKED_O`) from the Q gather's so the two could be mixed. G=1,
129 requests, ~6.9 items/CTA, handshake OFF:

| gather | store | bad rows | worst rel |
|---|---|---|---|
| packed | packed | **112 / 384** | 12.99 |
| packed | **stock** | 22 / 384 | 17.83 |
| **stock** | packed | 32 / 384 | 6.298 |
| **stock** | **stock** | **6 / 384** | 17.33 |

**RETRACTION: I reported stock+stock as "CLEAN 0/384" from a SINGLE RUN.** It is 6/384 here, on the
same build and config. So the multi-item path is racy **even with stock paths** -- mildly -- and the
claim that "the shared multi-item machinery is correct" is withdrawn. That is the single-sample
error I had already flagged twice today on this very defect, made a third time.

**What the matrix does support, with the baseline at ~6:**
- the packed **store** adds ~26 bad rows (32 vs 6);
- the packed **gather** adds ~16 (22 vs 6);
- **both together give 112, not ~48** -- strongly superlinear. They interact, which fits a shared
  smem region: `sQ` and `sO` both live in the aliased storage and are both reused per work item, so
  each one's unordered reuse widens the other's window.

**So there are at least three contributors** -- a small baseline race present even in stock paths,
plus the gather and the store, which compound. No single fix will close this; and the earlier
"handshake halves it" and "stock is clean" readings were each one sample on a racy configuration.

**Method correction I should carry: every arm of a racy defect needs a repeat count before it is
read.** Three times today I drew a conclusion from one run of a configuration whose failure rate is
a few percent -- the 5/5 and 8/8 "mixed-only" claim, the 0/35 "closed" claim, and now 0/384
"stock is clean". The fix is procedural: for this defect, no arm counts at n=1.

**Next, and sized properly:** re-run all four corners x10 to get rates rather than points, then
attack the largest contributor. `write_packed`'s per-row scalar loop reading `sO` is the leading
candidate, and it is also what the reverted 12% parallelisation touched -- which now reads as a
third signal pointing at the same code.

**[x] ISOLATED (2026-10-10): the multi-item defect is in OUR PACKED PATHS. Stock paths are CLEAN. [SUPERSEDED by the four-corner bisect above]
And my handshake is NOT the fix -- it has its own bug.**

Full matrix at G=1 (where `FUSED_PACKED_Q=off` is a valid comparison), 129 requests, ~6.9 work
items per CTA, all-FA3, `SM_SPLIT=all`:

| arm | bad rows | worst rel |
|---|---|---|
| **stock TMA Q + `write_tiled`, handshake OFF** | **0 / 384 CLEAN** | 0.002224 |
| stock paths, handshake ON | 10 / 384 | 18.07 |
| our packed gather + `write_packed`, handshake OFF | **144 / 384** | 15.25 |
| our packed paths, handshake ON | 96 / 384 | 15.47 |
| our packed paths at G=4 (production default) | 116 / 384 | 11.04 |

**Two conclusions, both load-bearing:**

1. **The shared multi-item machinery is correct.** With stock's TMA Q load and `write_tiled`, a CTA
   looping over ~7 work items at 129 requests is CLEAN (0/384). So the scheduler, `get_next_work`,
   `counter`, the `barrier_Q` phase and the epilogue dispatch all handle cross-item reuse fine.
   **The defect is OURS**: the packed-Q gather and/or `write_packed`, which reuse `sQ` and `sO`
   across items without the ordering stock gets from TMA transaction counts and TMA store
   semantics.
2. **My store-completion handshake is NOT the fix, and it is actively harmful.** It helps the
   packed path (144 -> 96) but breaks a previously CLEAN arm (stock: 0 -> 10). So it mitigates one
   hazard while introducing another -- almost certainly an arrival-count asymmetry on a `continue`
   path I believed symmetric. **It should be reverted rather than defaulted on**; a partial
   mitigation that corrupts a clean configuration is worse than nothing.

**This also re-reads the earlier "handshake halves the corruption" result correctly.** 112 -> 56 at
G=4 looked like progress toward a fix. In fact the baseline it halved was itself caused by the
packed paths, and the same flag damages the stock path. The halving was real; the interpretation
("the handshake is the required fix") was wrong.

**The fix direction is now clear and matches stock:** give the packed paths the same ordering
guarantees TMA provides -- either arm `barrier_Q` with a transaction count the gather actually
satisfies (`arrive_and_expect_tx` over the gathered bytes, rather than
`cpasync_barrier_arrive_noinc` on a count-armed barrier), or route the packed O store through TMA
and restore `tma_store_wait<0>()`. Both are what `FA2+FA3 co-inclusion` already told us: deviating
from 0.7's primitives is where this port's bugs live.

**[!] `kQueryEmpty` hypothesis REFUTED by direct comparison with stock 0.7.** Both sides are
byte-identical to stock:
- producer (`sparse_mainloop.cuh`): `NamedBarrier::sync(NUM_MMA_THREADS +
  Ktraits::NUM_PRODUCER_THREADS, kQueryEmpty)` -- identical;
- consumer (`mainloop_mma.cuh`): `NamedBarrier::arrive(NUM_MMA_THREADS +
  Ktraits::NUM_PRODUCER_THREADS, kQueryEmpty)` -- identical;
- plus stock's one-off `mma_init()` arrival on the same barrier.

Arrival arithmetic checks out: 256 MMA threads arrive + 128 producer threads sync = 384 =
`NUM_MMA_THREADS + NUM_PRODUCER_THREADS`. So the packed-Q gather did NOT break this handshake, even
though it replaced the TMA Q load wholesale.

**`work_idx` symmetry also checks out**, which was hypothesis (2): both loops skip `++work_idx` on
the *same* two `continue` paths (tile out of range; `num_kv_tiles <= 0`), so the `barrier_Q` phase
(`work_idx % 2`) cannot drift between producer and consumer.

**So the remaining half is not in either Q handshake.** The next step should be the A/B that has
worked repeatedly rather than more inspection: **run the multi-item fixture with
`FUSED_PACKED_Q=off` at G=1**, i.e. the stock TMA Q load and stock `write_tiled`, through the same
scheduler. That isolates "our packed paths" from "the port's multi-item plumbing" in one run:
- still corrupt => the defect is in the shared multi-item machinery (scheduler/epilogue reuse), and
  the packed paths are innocent;
- clean => it is in the packed gather or `write_packed` when `sQ`/`sO` are reused across items.

Command shape (needs a G=1 multi-row fixture, i.e. `mix_decode` with `GQA1=1`):
`MODE=mix_decode DEC_ROWS=128 MIX_ALL_FA3=1 GQA1=1 FUSED_PACKED_Q=off FA3_MBARRIER=0 O_HANDSHAKE=1`.

**Left OFF by default** until it is a complete fix: a flag that halves a correctness bug is worse
than useless as a default, because it makes the remaining failures rarer and therefore harder to
catch.

**Note what this invalidates:** the "race CLOSED, 0/35 co-resident" result stands only for
<= 1 item per CTA. On realistic batch shapes (a chunk plus ~100 decode rows) the kernel is
**incorrect**, so **no serving arm can be run until the handshake lands**.

**Priority note:** this is a correctness defect on the *most realistic* batch shape tested so far
(a prefill chunk plus ~100 decode rows), which is precisely the 4-mode serving shape. It outranks
the FA2 perf work, because a serving arm on this shape would be wrong, not just slow.

### [!] DECODE-HEAVY ARM REVERSES IT: on realistic 4-mode shapes the fusion is **NET NEGATIVE**

The +5.4% below was measured on a batch with **2 decode tokens**. I predicted the margin would GROW
with more co-resident FA2 work. **It inverts.** One prefill chunk (256 x 2048) plus N decode rows
(1 x 2048), all arms 0 bad rows except where noted, 30 iters / 8 warmup:

| decode rows | co-resident, best `sm_split` | all-FA3 control (same rows) | fusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 (the old arm) | 0.2426 @128 | 0.2557 | **+5.4%** |
| **8** | 0.3665 @96 | **0.2512** | **1.46x SLOWER** |
| **32** | 0.7371 @64 | **0.3670** | **2.01x SLOWER** |
| 128 | 2.6314 @64 | *control FAILED, see below* | — |

Per-split detail at dec=32: 0.7371 (64), 1.2568 (96), 2.0489 (112), **8.6806** (128). At dec=8:
0.4514 (64), 0.3665 (96), 0.5485 (112), 2.2380 (128). Note the best `sm_split` MOVES DOWN as decode
grows (128 -> 96 -> 64) and the penalty for getting it wrong explodes -- 8.68 ms at dec=32 /
split=128, 23x worse than that shape's own optimum.

**Why, and it follows from A3:** decode rows routed to FA2 land on an executor that is 3.7-5x
slower per row. The "spare SMs are free" argument fails because FA2 becomes the **critical path** --
the FA3 role finishes its one chunk and waits. So the more decode work the batch has, the worse
fusion does, monotonically.

**So the +5.4% was an artifact of a degenerate shape**: with only 2 decode tokens there was almost
no FA2 work to be slow, and offloading them freed the FA3 role. Retracted as a representative
number -- it is the best case, not the typical one, and a real 4-mode step has many decode rows.

**The project-level conclusion, stated plainly: the two-role FA3+FA2 fusion as implemented is
net-negative on realistic 4-mode batches.** It is not a tuning problem -- at dec=32 no `sm_split`
reaches the all-FA3 control. The fusion can only pay if the FA2 role reaches rough parity with FA3,
and the FA2 role is currently **1.1x-22x off `BatchAttention`** (the same kernel family it was
ported from). **Fixing the FA2 role is therefore a precondition for the fusion mattering at all**,
not an optimisation after the fact.

**[!] NEW BUG found by the control arm: all-FA3 with 129 requests returns 92/384 bad rows.** Every
other arm in this sweep is 0 bad. So the FA3 path breaks at high request count -- untested before
because no fixture had more than 3 requests. That invalidates the dec=128 comparison and needs
isolating (suspect the plan's per-request arrays or the merge layout at scale).

### [x] THE FUSION QUESTION, MEASURED DIRECTLY (2026-10-10): co-residency is worth **+5.4%**

Never measured before. Same rows (`qo=[256,1,1]`, `kv=[2048,300,512]`), both arms 0 bad rows,
40 iters / 10 warmup:

| config | ms |
|---|---|
| co-resident (`mixed`, FA3+FA2) @ `SM_SPLIT=96` | 0.3228 |
| @ 112 | 0.2604 |
| @ 120 | 0.2579 |
| **@ 128 (best)** | **0.2426** |
| **FA3-only, all SMs** (same rows, everything routed to FA3) | **0.2557** |
| FA3-only @ 128 | 0.2570 |

**Fusion beats routing-everything-to-the-better-kernel by 1.054x, i.e. +5.4%.** So co-residency
does pay -- which answers the question A3's sweep raised -- but the margin is 5.4%, not 30%.

**What that implies for the bar, and it is the most consequential number in the project.** The
>=30% TTFT/ITL target is end-to-end. Attention is **20.5%** of step time (B1b). A 5.4% win on
attention is therefore **~1.1% end-to-end** -- two orders below the bar, and well inside the
+/-1.5-3% serving noise floor, meaning **it would not even be measurable in a serving A/B**.

**Caveat that bounds it, and it points at the one arm that could change the answer:** this batch
has only **2 decode tokens** against a 256-token prefill chunk, so there is almost nothing for the
FA2 role to overlap. Fusion's value should grow with the amount of co-resident FA2 work. **The
missing arm is a decode-heavy mix** -- e.g. one prefill chunk against 32-128 decode rows, which is
closer to a real 4-mode step -- where the FA2 role has enough work that overlapping it is worth
more than 5.4%. That is the arm to run before concluding the kernel route is capped, and it is now
the single highest-value measurement left.

**What is already fixed regardless:** at every `sm_split` tested, co-resident beats FA3-only only
at 128 (0.2426 vs 0.2557); at 96 it is *worse* (0.3228). So the fusion's win is entirely contingent
on getting `sm_split` right, and the default of 16 was 6.2x off. SM pre-assignment is not a
refinement of the fusion -- it is the thing that makes it positive at all.
